en: Even now, I think of her, fair as a garland of golden campaka flowers, with a face like a full-blown lotus and a slender line of body hair; she who has just awakened, her limbs languid and overwhelmed by passion, like a sacred lore multiplied through negligence.
If I were to see once again that moon-faced woman, rich in fresh youth, with full breasts and a fair complexion,
her limbs tormented by the fire of the arrows of Love, I would now make my own limbs perfectly cool.
Even now, if I were to see again that lotus-eyed woman, weary from the weight of her full breasts,
I would press her face with my two arms and drink from it at will, like a mad bee drinking from a lotus.

Even now, I remember her, her limbs exhausted by the fatigue of lovemaking, with a mass of curls fallen upon her pale cheeks, her creeper-like arms entwined around my neck as she moved slowly, burdened by the secret of her sin.

Even now, at dawn, I remember that long-eyed woman, her face bowed with shame— the royal swan in the lotus pond of the essence of love— her tremulous pupils rolling askance as she reeled from staying awake throughout the night of passion.
If even now I should again behold that woman with eyes as long as the span of my ear, her slender body feverish from the long separation,
then embracing her firmly with my limbs, I would not open my eyes nor would I let her go.

Even now, I remember her— the director of the dance of love, whose face is as beautiful as the full moon, whose limbs are languid with intoxication, who is slender yet bowed by the weight of her broad hips and breasts, and who possesses a mass of disheveled, dangling locks.

Even now, I remember her on the bed, her pervasive fragrance arising from the scent of musk mixed with smooth sandalwood paste, her lovely eyes beautiful with lashes clinging together as they kissed one another’s beaks.

Even now, I remember her during our lovemaking—red with wine, possessing playful lips, slender of body, with tremulous and long eyes; her limbs anointed with saffron paste and musk, and her mouth filled with camphor and betel nut.

Even now, I remember the face of my beloved, its limbs anointed with golden-hued unguents and covered with a multitude of sweat-drops; with eyes rolling from the exhaustion of passion, it resembles the orb of the moon just released from an eclipse by Rāhu.

Even now, that scene revolves in my mind: when I was hungry at night, the princess, out of anger, rejected the auspicious greeting "Live long! and, without speaking, placed a golden leaf behind her ear.
Even now, I remember the face of my beloved during the exertion of inverted union— her cheeks rubbed by golden earrings,
with large, distinct drops of perspiration from the fatigue of swaying, scattered like a profusion of pearls.

Even now I remember her heavy glance, born from the pain of my rejection; her graceful arching of the body in the confusion of passion; the beautiful curve of her breasts as they brushed against the hem of her garment; and her lip, adorned with the marks of my teeth and nails.

Even now, I remember my beloved, whose hands are red as the fresh sprouts of the *aśoka* tree, whose nipples are kissed by clusters of pearls, whose cheeks are pale with a suppressed smile within, and who possesses the graceful gait of a swan.

Even now I remember the mark of her fingernail-scratches, impressed upon her thighs thick with golden dust; and I recall how, as she rose, she grasped the shimmering golden garment she had pulled off, holding it in her hand as she walked away out of shame.

Even now, in private, I remember her with eyes tremulous from applied collyrium, with a mass of hair thick with many flowers, with the luster of teeth like pearls mingled with vermilion, and wearing golden bracelets.

Even now, I remember her in private— her mass of hair with its bonds loosened, her garland slipped, her lower lip sweet with the nectar of her smile, her pearl necklace shimmering as it kissed the slope of her full, high breasts, and her eyes darting restlessly.

Even now, I think of her in that white chamber, where darkness was dispelled by the mass of rays from rows of jewel-lamps; she who, having made an effort to see me face-to-face in secret, had her eyes filled with shame, fear, and longing.

Even now I remember her, whose limbs are tormented by the fire of separation—she who is slender, with eyes like those of a deer, the sole vessel for sexual delight; she who wears various and wonderful ornaments, whose gait is like that of a royal swan, and who possesses beautiful teeth.

Even now, I remember her as she smiled, bent by the weight of her breasts, her neck made white by a string of pearls— the beloved of the flower-armed god on Mount Mandara during his play, the beautiful banner of his radiant and brilliant flower-weapon.

Even now, I remember the speech of my beloved, who was exhausted by the fatigue of love-making; it was a discourse rendered charming by its indistinct sounds, uttered with a faltering voice, and composed of words mixed together, yet perfectly suited to the meaning of her hundreds of playful endearments.

Even now, even in another life and even at the moment of death, I think of her— her eyes closed in the intoxication of love, her slender body relaxed, her garments and tresses disheveled, she who was like a royal swan in the forest of the lotuses of the erotic sentiment.

Even now, if at the close of day I might once again behold that beloved one with eyes like a young fawn’s, bearing a pair of jar-like breasts filled with nectar, I would renounce the pleasures of heaven, liberation, and the realm of men.

Even now, I remember that beloved, who was the foremost and peerless model among all beautiful women on earth for the perfection of every limb; she was the drinking vessel for the finest essence of the erotic sentiment in dramas, yet she was pained by the arrows of the flower-weaponed god of love.

Even now, I do not for a moment forget that girl— clinging to my body like a wet garment, her frame tormented by the fire of passion and my own mature majesty, helpless and pitiable, yet dearer to me than life itself.

Even now, O people, I reflect with the thought: "This fire of separation from my daughter—the princess who was fashioned as the sole vessel for the affection of the most beautiful women from the very beginning—is impossible to endure. (BiCaup_26)
Even now, leaving aside the gods, my mind forcibly moves toward her who causes such wonder; what can I do?
For even though I know that at this time of death she will vanish moment by moment, my firm resolve remains: "She is lovely," "She is most dear," "She is mine."
Even now, I recall her—her eyes as tremulous as those of a frightened doe at the mere mention of my departure;
her speech faltering, her eyes clouded with falling tears, and her face bowed down by heavy grief.
Even now, though I have striven with great skill, I have never once seen a face so beautiful that it rivals hers—
she who has surpassed Rati in loveliness with the splendor of the moon, and who possesses the great quality of extreme purity.

Even now, I remember her—whose momentary separation is comparable to poison, yet whose embrace is a far more abundant consecration of nectar; she who sustains my life, who is the parasol against the heat of passion, with her mass of disheveled hair and beautiful teeth.
Even now, as I am being led away from the bedchamber by those resembling the messengers of Yama with their irresistible and terrifying hands,
my mind is distressed, thinking of what various things she did not do for my sake— things that cannot possibly be told.

Even now, by day and by night, my heart is tormented because I no longer behold before me, at every step, the face of my beloved, which is as beautiful as the full moon and which, with its loveliness, surpassed Rati, destroyed Kama’s pride, and healed his wounds.

Even now, with an unwavering mind, I contemplate that young woman who was my hope for life—she whose essence was the fresh burden of youth never enjoyed by another; may she alone be my refuge even in another birth, so that it may be so.

Even now, the resonance of the bracelets on her sprout-like hands as she playfully waves them still completely enraptures my mind— she whose cheeks are kissed by swarms of bees wandering about, greedy for the fragrance of her lotus-face.

Even now I remember that mark of my fingernail upon the circle of her breast, which was given by me while I was intoxicated by drinking her honeyed breath; it remains awake, guards it, and watches over it with its many bristling hairs standing on end.

Even now, though her face has been turned away by anger and she is unwilling to speak, as soon as I press my face to hers, she weeps bitterly; I fall at her feet, "O beloved, you are my mistress, favor me—I remember [my transgression]."

Even now my mind runs away; what can I do? Even though I am with my friends in the bedchamber at this lovely hour—where there is the joy of play, the touch of a lover’s body, laughter, and various dances—let my time pass in such delights.

Even today, no one in this world is able to describe her, for she has no equal; she is my chosen bride. Indeed, if there were any man who had seen the form of those two who are so alike, he alone—and no other—would be capable of doing so.
Even now, I truly do not know whether she is the wife of a lord who has fallen by a curse, or perhaps the splendor of the Lord of the Gods;
or was she created by the Creator himself for the sake of deluding the world, or out of a desire to behold that jewel among young women?

Even now, for the sake of a joke, look at that collyrium on your eyes, your radiant face, and your ears resting at ease; though your body has grown thin due to your two new breasts, there is no fault if it should perish.
Even now, her face—possessing the radiant luster of the stainless autumnal moon—could steal away the heart of even a sage, let alone mine;
if I were to obtain it, which is composed of nectar, I would kiss and drink from it incessantly, for it agitates my mind.

Even now, if I could once again attain that singular sacred ford of sexual union— which is fragrant with the scent of lotus pollen, whose waters are love itself, and which brings about the downfall of the god of love— I would surely give up my life for the sake of attaining it.

Even now, alas, though this world is filled with hundreds of thousands of beauties who possess one another’s supreme qualities in abundance, the thought remains in my heart that her form cannot be compared even to others, let alone to me. (BiCaup_43)
Even now, that river of my mind remains ever-present, its vast nature shimmering with waves of horripilation;
like a beloved royal swan possessing the luster of a kadamba filament, she tells me of the exhaustion of her limbs and the wounds upon her eyes.

Even now, that beloved royal swan— her limbs beautiful with fresh youth, her slender body shimmering with the waves of horripilation— emerges slightly from the deep mire of the intense separation moving within my heart.

Even now, O King, I think of that princess, the crest-jewel of royalty, whose eyes roll languidly with the intoxication of full youth—like a daughter of the Gandharvas, Yakṣas, gods, Kinnaras, or Nāgas fallen from heaven, alas! BiCaup_45.

Even now, I cannot forget her— her waist as slender as a sacrificial altar, her pair of jar-like breasts filled with lofty nectar, her limbs adorned with various wonderful ornaments— as she rises from sleep at night or by day.

Even now, I remember that woman who was like a life-restoring medicine— her limbs languid with intoxicating beauty, trembling with bashful longing as if she were falling down, and rendered faint by the kisses born from the contact of our bodies.

Even now, I remember her tender yet firm passion during that hand-to-hand combat of amorous play— a battle where hands were rendered empty by the constant falling and rising of entwined limbs, and which was drenched with blood from the biting of lips and the scratching of nails.
"Even now I live only by the enjoyment of sexual union with my excellent bride, and not by any other means for even a single moment.
Therefore, brothers, death alone is the means to pacify my suffering; I entreat you, cut it off quickly! (BiCaup_49)
Even today, it is said that Hara does not cast off the Kālakūṭa poison; the Tortoise indeed bears the earth upon his back;
and the ocean carries the unbearable submarine fire. The virtuous protect that which they have once undertaken.
